findings.title: `react/no-danger` set to "warn" contradicts stated intent
findings.desc: The block's comment says these rules "fail loudly if a future change tries to weaken any of those", but `react/no-danger` is only a warning, so introducing `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` will not fail `npm run lint`/CI unless lint runs with `--max-warnings=0`; either set it to "error" or fix the comment.

findings.title: `trust: true` selector is trivially bypassed
findings.desc: `Property[key.name='trust'][value.value=true]` only matches an identifier key with a literal `true`, so `{ "trust": true }`, `{ trust: !!1 }`, `{ trust: () => true }`, or `trust` supplied via a variable/spread all slip through, which undercuts the comment claiming the selector is "broad enough" to be a reliable guardrail.

findings.title: rehype-raw restriction misses subpaths and non-static imports
findings.desc: `paths: [{ name: "rehype-raw" }]` does not match `rehype-raw/lib/...`, `require("rehype-raw")`, or dynamic `import()`; adding a `patterns: ["rehype-raw", "rehype-raw/*"]` entry would close the obvious gaps.

findings.title: `npm audit` makes CI non-deterministic and duplicated
findings.desc: The step hits the registry on every push/PR (and runs twice, once per Node matrix entry), so a newly published high-severity advisory in a prod dep breaks unrelated branches — the exact failure mode the comment claims to avoid by using `--audit-level=high`.

findings.title: `react/no-danger` set to "warn" contradicts the "fail loudly" intent
findings.desc: The block comment says these rules "fail loudly if a future change tries to weaken" the XSS posture, but `react/no-danger` is `warn`, so a newly added `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` will pass `npm run lint` (no `--max-warnings=0` in CI) and land silently; use `"error"` for parity with the other two rules.

findings.title: `trust` selector is narrower than the comment claims
findings.desc: `Property[key.name='trust'][value.value=true]` misses the string-key form (`"trust": true`, where the key is on `key.value`) and, more importantly, misses KaTeX's function form (`trust: () => true`, `trust: ctx => ctx.command === '\\href'`) and any truthy non-literal (`trust: flag`), so the comment "broad enough to catch `{ trust: true }` elsewhere too" overstates the guardrail's coverage.

findings.title: rehype-raw restriction is easily bypassed
findings.desc: `no-restricted-imports` with `paths` only matches the exact specifier, so `import rehypeRaw from "rehype-raw/lib/index.js"`, `require("rehype-raw")`, or a dynamic `import("rehype-raw")` are not flagged; a `patterns: ["rehype-raw", "rehype-raw/*"]` entry (plus a `no-restricted-syntax`/require rule) would actually close the hole the comment claims to close.

findings.title: audit step makes CI failures time- and network-dependent
findings.desc: `npm audit` is run once per matrix Node version and depends on the live registry, so unrelated PRs can fail (or flake) whenever a new high-severity advisory is published; consider a single non-matrix job or a scheduled workflow so functional CI stays deterministic.

findings.title: `react/no-danger` as "warn" does not enforce anything
findings.desc: The block comment claims these rules "fail loudly if a future change tries to weaken" the XSS posture, but `warn` does not fail `npm run lint` (no `--max-warnings=0` in CI), so a newly introduced `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` would pass CI with only a warning; use `"error"` (or add `--max-warnings 0`).

findings.title: `trust: true` selector is easy to bypass unintentionally
findings.desc: `Property[key.name='trust'][value.value=true]` only matches identifier keys with a boolean literal; it silently misses `{ "trust": true }` (string key uses `key.value`), computed keys, `opts.trust = true` assignments, and truthy non-literals like `trust: 1` or `trust: someFlag` — consider adding `Property[key.value='trust'][value.value=true]` and an AssignmentExpression selector.

findings.title: rehype-raw ban has gaps
findings.desc: `paths` matches only the exact bare specifier, so `rehype-raw/lib/...` subpath imports, `require("rehype-raw")`, and direct use of the underlying `hast-util-raw` are not blocked; adding a `patterns` entry (e.g. `rehype-raw*`, `hast-util-raw*`) would make the guardrail match its stated intent.

findings.title: `--omit=dev` comment overstates coverage; step is duplicated across the matrix
findings.desc: In a Next.js app many devDependencies are compiled/bundled into shipped client and server output, so "only audit production deps (the ones that ship to users)" is inaccurate; additionally the audit runs once per Node version (20 and 22) with identical results and depends on the live advisory DB, so it adds redundant network work and can fail CI on branches unrelated to the change.
